1. Executive Project Summary (The Simple Story)

The Clinical Problem: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the world's #1 cause of mortality (17.9 million deaths annually). Most clinical machine learning papers claim "95%–99% accuracy" on small datasets, but these models almost universally collapse when tested on patients from another hospital because of data leakage and hospital distribution shift.

Our Research Question: Can a modern deep tabular neural network (Multi-Layer Perceptron) or a sophisticated hybrid stacking ensemble (HPEM) outperform established tree-based models (XGBoost), and do these predictions reliably transfer across different hospital systems?

The Core Headline Finding:
  • On the large outpatient screening cohort (Cardio70k, N=68,581), XGBoost achieved the best discriminative performance (ROC-AUC 0.8019, F1 0.7205), winning in 5 out of 5 outer folds during nested cross-validation.
  • Our Deep Neural Network (MLP) proved to be a highly competitive neural baseline (ROC-AUC 0.7991, F1 0.7203), significantly outperforming linear Logistic Regression (+0.0052 ROC-AUC, 95% CI [0.0040, 0.0065]) and matching XGBoost on clinical Net Benefit.
  • In the 5-center hospital generalization stress test (Unified Cohort, N=1,918), the complex foundation paper model (HPEM) overfit local clinics and collapsed to 0.6107 ROC-AUC, whereas regularized models generalized far better.
  • We discovered that adding explicit Missingness Indicators boosted cross-hospital generalization across every single tested model (raising Logistic Regression ROC-AUC from 0.7449 to 0.7653).

2. Datasets, Specifications & Provenance

A central scientific strength of this project is that we explicitly refused to concatenate incompatible datasets. We evaluated two separate clinical tracks:

Track A: Cardio70k Cleaned Cohort (Primary Large-Scale Screening Track)

  • Records & Features: 68,581 unique patients, 14 candidate clinical predictors, 1 binary target (0 = no CVD, 1 = CVD present).
  • Target Balance: 33,929 CVD-positive cases (49.47%) vs. 34,652 CVD-negative cases (50.53%). Near-perfect 50/50 balance.
  • Missing Values: Zero missing cells across all 68,581 records.
  • Predictors Used: Age (years), Sex (0=female, 1=male), Height (cm), Weight (kg), Systolic BP, Diastolic BP, Cholesterol Level (1: normal, 2: above normal, 3: well above normal), Glucose Level (1, 2, 3), Smoking status (0/1), Alcohol intake (0/1), Physical activity (0/1), BMI, Pulse Pressure (Systolic minus Diastolic), and BP Category.
  • Clinical Provenance: Derived from standard outpatient periodic health examinations in Russia (publicly archived for medical research). Fully anonymized, real physiological measurements.
  • Clinical Role: Outpatient primary prevention and routine cardiovascular screening.

Track B: Unified Multi-Center Clinical Dataset (Generalization Stress-Test Track)

  • Records & Sources: 1,918 patients collected across 5 international institutions in 4 countries:
    1. Mendeley India: 1,000 patients (58.0% positive)
    2. UCI Cleveland Clinic (USA): 303 patients (45.9% positive)
    3. UCI Hungarian Institute of Cardiology: 293 patients (36.2% positive)
    4. UCI Long Beach VA Medical Center (USA): 199 patients (74.4% positive)
    5. UCI University Hospital Zurich (Switzerland): 123 patients (93.5% positive)
  • Missingness: Highly heterogeneous and source-dependent (e.g., fluoroscopy vessels and thallium stress tests are frequently omitted in community centers).
  • Predictors: Age, Sex, Chest Pain Type (1–4), Resting Blood Pressure, Serum Cholesterol, Fasting Blood Sugar, Resting ECG, Maximum Heart Rate, Exercise Induced Angina, Oldpeak (ST depression), ST Slope, Number of Major Vessels, Thalassemia.
  • Clinical Role: Evaluating whether algorithms trained in one healthcare system survive transfer to another healthcare system with different demographics, equipment, and missing data.
Safety & Data Audit Decision (Auditing Extra ECG & Synthetic CT/MRI Archives):
Our workstation contained two extra archives: an ECG waveform archive (archive (3).zip, 4,998 rows) and a synthetic CT/MRI image archive (archive (4).zip, 30,352 image slices). We executed an audit script (audit_additional_datasets.py) and formally documented in reports/additional_dataset_suitability.md that the synthetic imaging data contained no disease labels and zero verified patient linkage to the clinical records.

Why this matters for your defense: Amateur projects often fabricate "multimodal" claims by randomly pairing images with clinical CSVs. By formally auditing and rejecting unlinked synthetic data, we upheld medical ethics and research integrity.

4. Plain-English Technical Glossary

Memorize these definitions so you can speak with authority if asked by examiners:

What is "Data Leakage"?
Data leakage occurs when information from outside the training dataset (such as the test set or future data) is inadvertently used to train the model. For example, if you calculate the mean blood pressure of all 70,000 patients and use it to fill missing values before splitting, your training data already "knows" about the test data. This inflates accuracy artificially in the lab, but the model crashes in real hospitals. We eliminated leakage by placing all preprocessing inside training folds.
What is "Nested Cross-Validation"?
Standard cross-validation uses the same test data to both pick the best model and evaluate its performance, creating optimistic bias. In Nested Cross-Validation, there is an "inner loop" (3 folds) that tests which model is best, and an "outer loop" (5 folds) that evaluates the winner on completely unseen patients. It is the gold standard in statistical machine learning.
What is "Leave-One-Source-Out" (LOSO) Evaluation?
Instead of randomly shuffling patients, we train the model on four hospital systems (e.g., India, Cleveland, Hungary, Switzerland) and test it on the fifth (Long Beach VA). We repeat this for each hospital. This directly simulates real-world deployment to an institution that the model has never encountered before.
What is "Hospital Distribution Shift" (Domain Shift)?
The phenomenon where patient demographics, disease severity, medical protocols, or measurement devices differ between hospitals. A model trained in Switzerland (where prevalence was 93.5%) will output distorted probability estimates when applied in Hungary (prevalence 36.2%).
What is "Probability Calibration" (ECE)?
A model might have high accuracy but produce terrible probabilities. If a model says 100 patients have an 80% risk of CVD, exactly 80 of them should actually have CVD. Expected Calibration Error (ECE) measures the gap between predicted probabilities and real-world event rates. Lower is better (0.00 is perfect).
What is "Decision Curve Analysis" (Clinical Net Benefit)?
Introduced in the British Medical Journal by Vickers & Elkin, DCA calculates the real-world clinical value of using a model. It balances the benefit of detecting true heart disease cases against the harm of false alarms (which trigger invasive angiograms or unnecessary medication) across decision thresholds.
What is a "Missingness Indicator"?
In medicine, missing data is rarely random. A doctor omits a test because the patient is too frail or because the clinic lacks equipment. A missingness indicator is an extra binary column (0 = test done, 1 = test omitted) that allows the algorithm to learn from the clinical act of omitting a test.

5. Evaluation Metrics Demystified

Metric Formula / Concept Clinical Meaning in Cardiology Our Achieved Result
Accuracy (TP + TN) / Total Overall percentage of correct predictions. Can be misleading if data is imbalanced. 73.58% (XGBoost)
Sensitivity (Recall) TP / (TP + FN) Critical: Percentage of sick patients correctly identified. High sensitivity prevents missed cardiac events. 68.83% (At 0.5 threshold)
Specificity TN / (TN + FP) Percentage of healthy patients correctly identified. High specificity avoids unnecessary angiograms. 78.22% (At 0.5 threshold)
Precision (PPV) TP / (TP + FP) When the algorithm sounds an alarm, what percentage actually has heart disease? 75.58%
F1-Score 2 × (Prec × Rec) / (Prec + Rec) Harmonic balance between precision and recall. 0.7205 (XGBoost) / 0.7203 (MLP)
ROC-AUC Area under True Positive vs False Positive curve Threshold-independent measure of ranking ability. 0.5 is coin flip, 1.0 is perfect. 0.8019 (XGBoost) / 0.7991 (MLP)
Brier Score Mean Squared Error of probabilities Measures accuracy of probabilistic confidence (0.00 is perfect, lower is better). 0.1802 (XGBoost)
ECE (10 Bins) Weighted calibration gap across deciles How closely predicted percentages match true disease occurrence. 0.0024 (Near-perfect on Cardio70k)

6. Machine Learning & Deep Learning Models Explained

We systematically benchmarked six distinct model paradigms under identical data partitions:

1. Logistic Regression (Linear Baseline)

Models the log-odds of CVD as a linear sum of weighted predictors. Highly interpretable, fast, and stable, but cannot capture complex interactions (e.g., high BP having worse impact only in older smokers) without manual interaction terms.

2. Random Forest (Bagging Ensemble)

Builds 250 deep decision trees on random subsets of patients and features, averaging their votes. Resilient to outliers, but can struggle with subtle continuous boundary shifts.

3. Histogram Gradient Boosting

Scikit-learn's optimized gradient boosting implementation that bins continuous features into 256 integer histograms. Extremely fast and natively robust to missing data.

4. XGBoost (The Winning Model)

Sequentially builds trees where each new tree corrects the residual errors of prior trees, using second-order gradients and L1/L2 tree regularization. Emerged as the overall champion (ROC-AUC 0.8019).

5. Multi-Layer Perceptron (Our Deep Learning Baseline)

A fully connected deep tabular neural network with two hidden layers: Input → Dense(128, ReLU) → Dense(64, ReLU) → Output(Sigmoid). Trained with Adam optimizer, batch size 256, L2 regularization (α=0.001), and early stopping. Proved that neural nets can match tree models on tabular CVD data (ROC-AUC 0.7991, F1 0.7203).

6. HPEM (Hybrid Polynomial Ensemble Model)

The architecture from our IEEE Access foundation paper (Al Gharib et al.): 2nd-degree polynomial feature expansion + Mutual Information selection of top 15 features + Soft-voting ensemble of RF, GB, and RBF-SVM + XGBoost meta-learner. We implemented a leak-free out-of-fold version.

9. Achievements, Limitations & Future Work

What Was Fully Achieved (100% Complete)

  • ✓ Data Provenance & Audit: Dissected 70,499 clinical records, validated ranges, verified target encoding, and audited external imaging archives.
  • ✓ Strict Leak-Free Pipeline: Implemented stratified and nested cross-validation with zero data leakage.
  • ✓ Neural Tabular Benchmark: Developed a regularized MLP, proving neural viability on large clinical tabular data.
  • ✓ Multi-Hospital Generalization: Tested models across five international clinical centers using Leave-One-Source-Out evaluation.
  • ✓ Replication of Foundation Paper (HPEM): Corrected meta-learner stacking leakage and proved HPEM fails to transfer across hospital centers compared to standard baselines.
  • ✓ Advanced Clinical Diagnostics: Implemented Expected Calibration Error, Permutation Importance, Subgroup 95% Wilson CIs, Missingness Indicators, and Decision Curve Analysis.

Scientific Limitations (Why Acknowledging Them Proves Maturity)

  1. Retrospective Data: Both cohorts consist of historical observations; prospective real-time hospital deployment has not been performed.
  2. Binary Biological Sex Legend: The underlying datasets record binary biological sex (0=female, 1=male), which does not capture broader gender identities.
  3. Lack of Valid Multimodal Image Linkage: Downloaded ECG and synthetic CT/MRI archives were excluded because they lacked clinical diagnosis labels and verified patient linkage.

Future Roadmap

  • Prospective clinical validation in collaboration with practicing cardiologists.
  • Integration of verified, patient-linked 12-lead ECG waveforms and echocardiogram imaging.
  • Development of dynamic calibration recalibrators that automatically adapt to local hospital prevalence.

10. Examiner Defense Q&A (Word-for-Word Speaking Script)

Q1: "Your accuracy is ~74% and ROC-AUC is 0.80. Why isn't it 95% or 98% like some published papers?"
Your Answer: "That is a critical distinction in clinical machine learning. High accuracy claims of 95%+ in the literature occur either because of post-diagnostic feature leakage (e.g., using angiogram results to predict heart disease) or severe methodological leakage, such as applying SMOTE or scaling before the train/test split. In our study, we evaluate 68,581 patients using only routine non-invasive screening vitals (blood pressure, cholesterol, glucose, age). Clinical risk scores like Framingham or ASCVD achieve ROC-AUCs around 0.75. An ROC-AUC of 0.802 on 68,581 patients with strict leak-free cross-validation represents the genuine physiological ceiling of routine vitals."
Q2: "What is your novel contribution if XGBoost beat your Deep Learning MLP?"
Your Answer: "Our contribution is data-centric and empirical, which is the gold standard in tabular data science today. First, we demonstrated via 300 paired bootstrap replicates that our MLP neural network statistically outperforms linear models (+0.0052 AUC, p<0.05) and matches XGBoost on F1 (0.7203 vs 0.7205) and clinical Net Benefit. Second, we conducted a multi-center stress test across five international hospitals, discovering that adding missingness indicators significantly improves hospital transfer. Third, we tested the foundation paper's HPEM architecture and showed it collapsed under cross-hospital transfer, providing a transparent negative result that advances clinical AI reproducibility."
Q3: "Why did you separate Cardio70k from the Unified Clinical Dataset instead of merging them?"
Your Answer: "Because they represent completely different clinical populations with incompatible feature schemas. Cardio70k is an outpatient screening physical with routine vitals and no missing data. The Unified dataset consists of hospital cardiology referrals with invasive diagnostic markers and heavy, clinic-specific missingness. Merging them would create artificial feature imputation artifacts and violate patient-cohort integrity. Keeping them separate allowed us to conduct a clean internal benchmark on Cardio70k and a true cross-hospital generalization stress test on the Unified cohort."
Q4: "Why did you exclude the downloaded ECG and CT/MRI datasets?"
Your Answer: "We executed a formal provenance and quality audit on both archives. The ECG archive lacked documented diagnostic labels and patient identifiers, while the synthetic CT/MRI archive contained no disease labels and zero linkage to the clinical records. Attempting to build a 'multimodal' model by randomly pairing unlinked synthetic images with clinical patients would be scientifically fraudulent. Excluding unlinked data preserves academic integrity."
Q5: "How would a doctor actually use this model in practice?"
Your Answer: "As demonstrated in our Decision Curve Analysis, the model should not be used as an autonomous diagnostic device, but as an early screening triage tool in primary care. A clinic can adjust the decision threshold—for example, setting the cutoff at 0.30 to achieve 88% sensitivity—to flag high-risk patients for secondary confirmatory tests (such as echocardiograms or coronary calcium scoring) while avoiding invasive procedures for low-risk patients."
